title: How to Handle A Student Who Yells At You
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by a reader's account of a student who suddenly yelled and accused her of favoritism during a game, Linsin lays out a four-step response for de-escalating confrontational outbursts: delay engaging with the complaint in the moment, calmly promising to "fix it" later; fix it by clarifying the relevant rule or procedure to the whole class after things calm down, without over-explaining to the individual student; enforce a stronger-than-usual consequence for brazen disrespect, potentially skipping the warning stage and involving parents or an administrator for serious incidents; and review the classroom's disrespect rule with the whole class a day or so later, since students often mirror behavior they've witnessed. He emphasizes minimizing direct contact with the offending student afterward, arguing that consistent, non-personal accountability — not conversations, apologies, or lecturing — is what ultimately earns back respect and even admiration.
points: Four-step de-escalation sequence for confrontational outbursts: Delay, Fix, Enforce, Review.
In the moment, delay engaging with an angry student's accusations rather than defending yourself directly — promise to "fix it" later and move on.
After things calm down, clarify the relevant rule to the whole class rather than over-explaining to the individual student.
Brazen disrespect warrants skipping the warning stage and may include parent notification or administrator referral for serious incidents.
Minimizing direct contact with the offending student afterward — letting consistent accountability do the talking — is framed as what earns back respect.
quotes: But then, out of the blue, a student stood up and accused her of favoring one team over another.
The instant you recognize—or think you recognize—a student becoming angry, your singular goal is to calm them down and avoid confrontation.

Instead, stay cool and relaxed, pretend it’s no big deal, and say “It’s okay. I understand what you’re saying. I can see how you might feel that way. I promise I’ll fix it, but let’s finish the game first.
You are under no obligation to explain yourself or your decisions to any student who speaks to you or approaches you disrespectfully —nor should you.

Any incident of brazen or continued disrespect should be met with your strongest consequence—which may include an extended time-out for elementary students or detention for high school students—plus a notification of parents.
As counterintuitive as it may seem, the less contact you have with the offending student, the less likely a similar incident will happen in the future.
